name: Rafael Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't go on anything. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm up at half four, at the Lindgren place by five for the morning milking. Ninety cows, a herringbone parlour, and I do the cups and the cleaning while Karl watches the numbers. Then it's feeding, scraping out, and this time of year I'm on the tractor carting muck or helping get the last of the potatoes into the store.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I was thirty-one years at the cardboard plant on Mill Road, on the corrugator line, until they shut it and moved it east. So I'm the old new boy. Karl's twenty years younger than me and he still has to show me the satellite steering on the big John Deere twice a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows, honestly. They know me now, they know my voice, and there's a cow called Pia who follows me around like a dog. What wears me out is my knees in winter, and feeling slow. At the plant I knew everything. Here I'm always the one asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always said at the plant: told you so. Every few years a salesman turns up promising a miracle machine, and then it's a slightly better gearbox. I'd say it in the union branch meeting and at the pub, not online, I don't do any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. My job's hands on, and if the clever computers stay clever on paper, then I'm milking cows till I'm sixty-seven. Karl uses an app for the herd records, and that's fine, that's his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep turning up at five, keep putting a bit by, about two hundred a month, into the savings like Ingrid and I do now. Maybe I'd finally get my tractor ticket for the bigger trailer, because that's useful whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weather forecast that turns out wrong in a good way. You put the waterproofs on for nothing and you're glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "told you so". Who would you be saying it to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bosses at the plant, mostly, in my head. They told us automation would save the factory, then they closed it anyway and moved it somewhere with cheaper wages. It wasn't a robot that took my job, it was a spreadsheet in head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that picture that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Holm farm next door. They put in a milking robot last year, a real one, the cow walks in and the arm finds the teats with a laser. That's not AI hype, that's already here, and my friend Josef got let go because of it. So even if the clever stuff fizzles, the machines are still coming for the cowshed.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, that the miracle machine turned out to be a better gearbox again. I'd say it at the union branch and the pub, never online.
S0.think: Privately it's a relief, because his work is hands-on and a plateau means milking until 67. But the milking robot next door that cost his friend Josef his job is a reminder that machines don't need clever AI to reach the cowshed.
S0.do: Keeps working the 5am milking at the Lindgren farm and keeps saving about 200 a month with his partner Ingrid. Plans to get his licence for the bigger trailer because it helps whatever happens.
S0.feel: Calm, like a bad forecast that didn't come true, with a small worry about the robot next door.
S0.quote: It wasn't a robot that took my job, it was a spreadsheet in head office.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael's distrust is aimed at owners and head offices, not at technology as such; the plant closure is the lens for everything. Even in the calmest picture he raises the milking robot at the Holm farm unprompted. The quiet admission that he feels slow and always has to ask colours how exposed he feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union in farming, not just in factories. If the farms are going to change how we work, the workers should have a say in how. I'd bring it up at the branch, and I'd tell the young lads at the market to sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it means the robot at Holm's comes to Lindgren's. Karl's a decent man, but he's got a bank loan on the new slurry tank, and if a robot is cheaper than me over five years, he'll do the sums. I'm the last one in and the slowest, so I'm the first one out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd push the branch to ask for a rule that farms bringing in robots have to retrain or keep older workers, or pay them out properly. I'd write to our member of parliament, on paper, I'm not doing email. And at home we'd stop the camper van fund and put it all into savings, maybe three hundred a month instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared yet, because it's a few years, but it's the same feeling as the last two years at the plant. You hear the rumours and you watch the managers' faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the first out. What would you tell Ingrid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight, the way I did when the plant letters came. She'd say, Rafael, you'll find something, and she'd be right that there are other farms round here. But I'm fifty-eight and I still can't drive the satellite steering without help, so who's taking me on over a twenty-five-year-old?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people in that picture learn to work alongside the new machines. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try if they paid for the course and didn't make me do it on a phone. But I'll be honest, I've never touched one of those AI things and I don't want to start. Every gadget I learned at the plant got replaced two years later anyway.

S1.say: I'd say this is why farm workers need a union, so we get a say in how the robots come in. I'd tell it to the branch and to the young lads at the market.
S1.think: He thinks the robot at the Holm farm will reach Lindgren's, and that Karl, with a loan on the slurry tank, will do the sums. As the last one hired and the slowest, he expects to go first.
S1.do: Pushes his union branch to demand retraining or proper payouts for older workers on farms that bring in robots, and writes a paper letter to his member of parliament. Stops the camper van fund and raises savings from about 200 to 300 a month.
S1.feel: Anxious, with the familiar feeling from the plant's last two years of watching managers' faces for clues.
S1.quote: I'm the last one in and the slowest, so I'm the first one out.
S1.fieldNote: The steady picture hits harder for Rafael than the label suggests, because it lines up with something he's already seen happen to his friend. His answer is collective, not personal: union rules and a letter to his MP before any retraining. He'd accept a course only if it's paid for and not on a phone, a real limit rather than a pose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that someone chose, and the people who chose it should pay for it. Tax the robot makers and the big farm companies, and pay people like me until our pensions start. I'd be at every meeting and every protest in the market square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I'm finished at sixty. Two years isn't enough time for anything, not for me to learn a new trade, not for the government to sort out a plan. I'd have four, maybe five months of savings, and then it's Ingrid's wage from the school kitchen, and the robots will be cooking there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd go full time on the union side, help organise every farm worker in the district before it hits. We'd cut everything, the car goes down to one, no holiday, and I'd ask my daughter Mette whether we could lean on her if it came to it, which I'd hate. When it arrives, I'd sign on for whatever support there is, without shame, because I paid in for forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the plant closing again, but this time there's no farm to run to afterwards. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Karl to tell me honestly what his plans are. Then I'd go to the branch secretary, Annika, and say we need a list of every farm worker over fifty-five in the district, names and phone numbers. When the plant closed we found out too late and everyone scattered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign on without shame. Is that how you'd really feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it without shame. Inside, no, it would sting. My father never took a penny from anyone, and I'd hear his voice. But I'd still do it, because the shame belongs to the people who sold the robots, not to me.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disaster somebody chose, and they should pay for it by taxing the robot makers and the big farm companies. I'd be at every meeting and every protest in the square.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be finished at 60, with no time to learn a trade and only four or five months of savings. Ingrid's school kitchen job wouldn't be safe either.
S2.do: Throws himself into organising every older farm worker in the district through the union branch within the first month, and cuts the household to one car and no holidays. Signs on for government support once it hits and may ask his daughter Mette for help.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, like the plant closing again but with nowhere left to run to.
S2.quote: The shame belongs to the people who sold the robots, not to me.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks Rafael's plan; two years leaves no runway to his pension at 67. Publicly he says he'd claim support without shame, privately he admits it would sting and hears his father. His instinct is still to build a list and organise, the lesson he took from the plant scattering too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really, but I'd have more time to say it. I'd want the union and the farmers' groups on the same side for once, asking for a proper plan for rural areas. That's what I'd say at meetings, that we've got five years and no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years gets me to sixty-three. That's closer, but it still leaves four years before the pension with nothing coming in. It might mean Karl keeps me on a bit longer while the robots are expensive, and then lets me go when they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and keep the cut-back budget going from day one, saving the three hundred a month, so by the time it lands we've got maybe a year's money instead of four months. I'd push the branch for an early-pension deal for farm workers over sixty. And I'd ask Karl, man to man, if he'd keep me on for the jobs a robot can't do, like the calving at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but I can breathe. It's more like the slow one than the fast one. I'd have a plan, even if I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. Thirty-six months of saving is about ten thousand, give or take, and that's a year of bills. And time for the union to win something. Two years isn't long enough for politicians to even hold the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Tomas. He's thirty and he drives a forklift at the big distribution warehouse by the motorway. If robots can milk a cow, they can drive a forklift. I'd worry more about him than me, actually, because he's got thirty years left to work.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years and no excuse, and that the union and the farmers' groups need to stand together for a proper plan for rural areas.
S3.think: Five years takes him to 63, still four years short of his pension. He expects Karl to keep him while robots are expensive and let him go once they're cheap.
S3.do: Keeps milking and saves about 300 a month from day one, aiming for roughly a year of bills by the time AGI lands. Pushes the branch for an early-pension deal for farm workers over 60 and asks Karl to keep him on for night calving.
S3.feel: Still anxious, but able to breathe because there's time to make a plan he doesn't like.
S3.quote: If robots can milk a cow, they can drive a forklift.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turns into money he can count: about ten thousand saved and time for the union to win something. His worry moves outward, to his son Tomas at the warehouse. He still won't consider retraining himself; his whole plan is a bridge to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this decently, so if they don't, it's because they didn't want to. That's the line I'd take at the branch. There's no excuse for anyone being thrown on the scrap heap with a decade's notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's almost a different story. Ten years takes me to sixty-eight, and I'm planning to stop at sixty-seven. So I might just squeeze through, milking cows until the day I get my pension, and the robots arrive the year after I've gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Lindgren's, keep saving the two hundred, maybe put the camper van fund back. I'd still spend my evenings on the union, but I'd be fighting for the young ones, not me. And I'd sit Tomas down and tell him to get a trade a robot can't do yet, though I couldn't tell you what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anything. I'd feel lucky, and a bit guilty about feeling lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Guilty about what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get out and Josef's lad and Tomas wouldn't. At the plant, the older men got their redundancy and the young ones got nothing. I always said that wasn't fair, and here I'd be, the older man getting out the door just in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about your own plans, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd try the course after all, if the union ran it. Not the computer side, but how to look after the robots, clean them, fix the simple things. Someone has to muck out the robot, and I've mucked out worse.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this decently, so if people are thrown on the scrap heap it's because nobody wanted to prevent it.
S4.think: Ten years takes him to 68, and he plans to stop at 67, so he may just squeeze through to his pension before robots arrive at the farm.
S4.do: Carries on at the Lindgren farm, keeps saving about 200 a month and may restart the camper van fund. Spends evenings on union work for younger workers and might take a union-run course on basic robot cleaning and care.
S4.feel: Uneasy, feeling lucky and a bit guilty about being lucky.
S4.quote: Someone has to muck out the robot, and I've mucked out worse.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's warning Rafael's own risk falls away and he turns to younger workers, echoing his anger at how the plant treated the young. The guilt about getting out just in time was the most honest moment. For the first time he opens the door to a course, but only practical, hands-on and run by the union.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd be sixty, with four months in the bank and nothing else I know how to do. What would help is a bridge to the pension for people like me, paid by the companies selling the robots, and a union strong enough to sit at the table when the robots come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Nobody ever does. A robot can find a teat with a laser, but Pia won't let anyone but me near her when she's calving. I spent thirty-one years being told the machines were coming for the factory. They did. I just didn't expect them to follow me out to the cowshed.

headlineQuote: I spent thirty-one years being told the machines were coming for the factory. They did. I just didn't expect them to follow me out to the cowshed.
portrait: Rafael Olsen is 58 and has been a hired hand on the Lindgren dairy and barley farm for three years, since the cardboard plant where he worked for 31 years shut down. He is still slow with the tractor's satellite steering, carries a flip phone, has never used an AI tool and has no plans to. He is a lifelong union man who blames owners and machine makers, not the people who lose out, and his answer to every scenario is to organise, vote and hold on until his pension at 67. He shrugs off a plateau, gets anxious about steady change because the neighbouring farm's milking robot already cost a friend his job, and is alarmed by fast AGI because he has no second career left in him. Ten years of warning eases him most, because it gets him close to his pension, though he worries about his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would hit at 60, years before his pension, with only about four months of savings and no other trade he could learn in time.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed bridge to the state pension for older workers pushed out by machines, paid for by the companies selling the robots, and a union strong enough to bargain over how the robots come in.
